A putting green on a Conway ranch lot's back forty feet

Conway's ranch lots run 8,000 to 12,000 square feet, big enough for a modest green without crowding the rest of the yard. Backyard putting greens here run $14–$30 per square foot as of September 2026, and the census-counted 13,596 residents of the CDP live mostly on lots old enough to carry real oak canopy.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Fitting a green onto an 8,000 to 12,000 sq ft ranch lot

A Conway lot in that size range usually leaves a rear yard wide enough for a contoured green plus fringe without the retaining walls or terracing a much smaller urban lot would need (lot-size figures for the Conway area). The 2020 Census counted 13,596 residents across the CDP (Census QuickFacts), a population built up mostly on that same ranch-era lot pattern rather than newer, narrower subdivision frontages, which is part of why a green here tends to sit comfortably rather than fighting the yard's shape.

Oak canopy old enough to reach into the layout

A canopy that's had sixty or seventy years to grow, common on Conway's original ranch lots, often reaches further into a backyard than a homeowner expects, and the state's turf rule keeps synthetic surfaces out of that drip line without a certified arborist's letter. Designing a green's breaks and tiers around an oak's actual canopy edge, not just its trunk, usually means shaping the layout before excavation starts rather than adjusting cups after a root gets found mid-dig.

Why washed rock matters more under a putting surface

The same rule requiring washed rock under any Conway lawn applies to a putting green's base, and the consequences of skipping it show up faster here than almost anywhere else on the property. Fines from unwashed fill binding into a crust don't just slow drainage the way they would under a lawn; they also create an uneven surface underneath the shaped tiers, which shows up as a dead spot or an unexpected bounce exactly where a ball should be rolling true. A green's fine tolerance for surface consistency makes a crusted, uneven base far more noticeable in daily use than the same problem would be under grass nobody's testing with a putter.

Why a green needs deeper excavation than a lawn

Excavation for a Conway green runs four to six inches, noticeably more than a flat lawn conversion covering the same square footage, because the extra depth makes room for a thicker, hand-shaped base without the finished green ending up perched above the surrounding turf. Too little depth and the shaped layers underneath can't hold their contours once the surface product goes on top; too much and the green sits in a shallow bowl that collects runoff from the lawn around it instead of shedding its own water outward. Confirming that number against the design before the first shovel of soil comes out saves a mid-project correction.

Say you have a 320 sq ft green tucked under live oak shade

A 320 square foot green fit into the shadier half of a Conway ranch backyard, common where an old oak already shades the spot a homeowner wants to putt, prices between $5,760 and $8,000 at the published $18–$25 typical range. If the oak's canopy actually overlaps part of that footprint, the arborist letter and the resulting layout change come before a number gets finalized, since the buildable shape can shift once the drip line is marked. A flatter, sunnier 320 square feet elsewhere on the same lot would price identically; shade changes contour planning and grooming, not the per-square-foot rate.

Keeping light infill from sliding down a tiered green

A Conway green's tiers create slopes a flat lawn never has to deal with, and infill brushed in at a light, even rate can still migrate slowly toward the lowest tier over months of rinsing and rain, thinning the higher ground while building up at the bottom. That's a version of the state's rule against infill leaving a property, just moving within the green's own footprint instead of off the lot entirely. A slightly heavier grooming pass on upper tiers during routine care, rather than a different infill product altogether, is usually enough to counter the drift before it changes how a ball rolls across the surface.

A green on the chain's edge answers to the same setback as any other turf

A putting green built on a lot backing onto the Conway chain still has to clear the state's 10-foot waterbody setback the same way a lawn or dog run does, waived only where a seawall already stands between the green and the water (the Lake Conway entry, 1,771 surface acres). That line gets staked during layout on a waterfront green specifically because losing ten feet off one edge can force the whole design, cups included, several feet inland from an original plan.

Our glossary of turf terms explains stimp speed and break design in more depth than a city page needs, and the putting green guide covers fringe and cup specs. Pine Castle, Edgewood and Hunters Creek all carry a similar ranch-era lot pattern a few minutes from the Conway hub.

A cup set too close to a tier's low point

Cups on a Conway green get cored after the base is shaped and confirmed to hold its breaks, and a cup placed right at or near a tier's lowest point can end up collecting a small amount of standing water after a storm even on a green that drains correctly everywhere else, since water naturally gathers there before it moves on. That's a design and placement issue rather than a base failure, and it's usually solved by shifting the cup a foot or two off the exact low point during layout rather than reworking the drainage underneath it. Catching this during the design stage, before coring, avoids relocating a finished cup later.

Rinsing a green for heat, dust, and grooming

A hose rinse on a Conway green does double duty: it drops surface temperature 30 to 50 degrees for more comfortable play on a hot afternoon, and it clears dust and pollen that would otherwise interfere with a clean, consistent roll. Rinsing before a grooming pass, rather than after, also helps the brush move infill more evenly, since damp infill settles differently than dry infill does under a stiff brush. This small sequencing choice, rinse first, then groom, makes routine maintenance slightly more effective without adding any extra steps to the routine itself.

Questions people ask

Do Conway's older oaks make a putting green harder to design than a newer subdivision's?

Sometimes. A decades-old canopy usually reaches further than a young tree's, which can eat into a planned green's footprint once the actual drip line gets marked, so it helps to walk the layout with the oak's real canopy edge in mind rather than a rough guess from the trunk.

Can a putting green go on a Conway lot that backs onto the lake chain?

Yes, outside the state's 10-foot waterbody setback unless a seawall already separates the lot from the water. That strip usually still leaves enough of an 8,000 to 12,000 square foot lot for a modest green once the buildable line is confirmed.
